# Weather instruments and forecasting (`weather_instruments`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: helped by atmospheric_pressure, thermometer_temperature, electric_telegraph, data_graphs
- Core idea: Weather can be measured and, a day or so ahead, foretold. A falling barometer warns of wind and rain, a fast fall of a storm; a rising one of fair weather. Storms are huge whirling systems hundreds of kilometres across that travel, in the middle latitudes mostly from west to east, so that yesterday's weather upwind is tomorrow's here. In the northern hemisphere, with the wind at your back, the low pressure lies to your left. Useful instruments: barometer, thermometer, a rain gauge (a straight-sided vessel, depth read with a ruler), a wind vane, and a hygrometer (a degreased hair or gut string that lengthens in damp air). Daily readings at fixed hours at many places, collected on one map, show the systems moving.
- Pitfalls:
  - Reading the barometer's level instead of its change
  - Promising forecasts weeks ahead or for an exact place and hour
  - Readings in the sun or at irregular times cannot be compared
  - Explaining weather by the Moon's phases or the planets
- History: india: c. 3rd c. BC–2nd c. AD – Arthashastra prescribes rain measurement in a standard bowl; china: c. 120 BC Huainanzi: charcoal on a balance shows humidity; wind vanes in use under the Han; 1247 Qin Jiushao on rain and snow gauges; east_asia: 1441–1442 – Korea: standard rain gauge (cheugugi) under Sejong, credited to the crown prince, issued to all provinces; greece: c. 340 BC Aristotle, Meteorologica; c. 50 BC wind vane on the Tower of the Winds; europe: c. 1450 Cusanus and Alberti describe hygrometer and anemometer; 1654 Medici network of observers; 1660 Guericke foretells a storm from the barometer; 1783 Saussure's hair hygrometer; 1820 Brandes' first weather maps; 1857 Buys Ballot's law; 1861 FitzRoy's telegraph-based storm warnings and forecasts; 1919 Bergen school, fronts; americas: 1743 – Franklin notes that storms travel against their own surface wind
- Read:
  - W. E. Knowles Middleton, Invention of the Meteorological Instruments (1969)
  - Peter Moore, The Weather Experiment (2015)
